title: Attestation Engagements (SSAE)
exam_relevance: MODERATELY TESTED - Expect 3-5 questions on CPA AUD exam about attestation engagements, particularly examination vs. review vs. AUP, SOC reports, and suitable criteria. Understanding SSAE is important for distinguishing from SSARS and audit engagements.
learning_objectives: Understand what constitutes an attestation engagement and how it differs from audit and SSARS engagements
Master the three types of attestation engagements: examination, review, and agreed-upon procedures (AUP)
Understand the concepts of subject matter, assertions, and suitable criteria in attestation
Know the requirements and characteristics of examination engagements (reasonable assurance)
Know the requirements and characteristics of review engagements (limited assurance)
Know the requirements and characteristics of agreed-upon procedures (no assurance, findings only)
Understand SOC (Service Organization Controls) reports: SOC 1, SOC 2, and SOC 3
Apply SSAE standards to determine appropriate attestation engagement type for various scenarios

introduction.overview: Statements on Standards for Attestation Engagements (SSAE) provide guidance for CPAs who perform attestation services on subject matter OTHER THAN historical financial statements. While audits (GAAS) and reviews/compilations (SSARS) deal with financial statements, SSAE deals with other types of subject matter.
introduction.what_is_attestation: An attestation engagement is one in which a CPA is engaged to issue a report on subject matter (or an assertion about subject matter) that is the responsibility of another party (usually management).

key_distinction.audit_GAAS: Audits of historical financial statements follow GAAS (Generally Accepted Auditing Standards - AU-C sections)
key_distinction.review_compilation_SSARS: Reviews and compilations of historical financial statements for non-public companies follow SSARS
key_distinction.attestation_SSAE: Attestation on OTHER subject matter (not historical FS, or special reports on FS) follows SSAE

introduction.key_standard: AT-C Section 105 (Concepts Common to All Attestation Engagements) and AT-C Section 205 (Examination Engagements), 210 (Review Engagements), and 215 (Agreed-Upon Procedures Engagements)
introduction.exam_importance: The CPA exam tests the differences between examination, review, and agreed-upon procedures attestation engagements, as well as understanding of SOC reports. You must distinguish SSAE from SSARS and GAAS.

fundamental_concepts.description: All attestation engagements involve three key components: subject matter, assertions, and criteria.

subject_matter.definition: The subject matter is what the attestation engagement is ABOUT - the phenomenon being measured or evaluated.
examples: Internal control over financial reporting (SOX 404 attestation)
Controls at a service organization (SOC reports)
subject_matter.not_subject_matter: Historical financial statements are NOT subject matter for SSAE - they're covered by GAAS (audits) or SSARS (reviews/compilations)
subject_matter.exam_note: If question asks about attestation on historical FS for non-public company, that's SSARS, not SSAE. SSAE is for OTHER subject matter.

assertions.definition: Assertions are declarations or claims made by management about the subject matter.
assertions.example: Management asserts 'Our internal controls over financial reporting are effective as of December 31, 2024.' The CPA attests to this assertion.
assertions.written_assertion: For examination and review engagements, management typically provides a WRITTEN assertion. For AUP, written assertion is not always required.

suitable_criteria.definition: Criteria are the standards or benchmarks used to evaluate or measure the subject matter. Criteria must be SUITABLE.
characteristics_of_suitable_criteria: RELEVANT - criteria must be relevant to the subject matter
OBJECTIVE - criteria should be free from bias
MEASURABLE - criteria should enable consistent measurement/evaluation
COMPLETE - criteria should include all relevant factors
AVAILABLE to users - users must be able to access the criteria to understand the report
examples_of_criteria: COSO Internal Control Framework (for control effectiveness attestation)
Debt covenant requirements specified in loan agreement (for compliance attestation)
AICPA Trust Services Criteria (for SOC 2 reports)
Custom criteria developed for specific engagement (if suitable)
suitable_criteria.importance: WITHOUT suitable criteria, the CPA cannot perform an attestation engagement. The criteria provide the 'ruler' for measuring the subject matter.
suitable_criteria.exam_emphasis: Questions may ask whether criteria are suitable or may describe a situation where criteria are missing or inappropriate. If criteria aren't suitable, CPA cannot accept the engagement.

practitioner_vs_responsible_party.responsible_party: The party responsible for the subject matter (usually management or those charged with governance)
practitioner_vs_responsible_party.practitioner: The CPA performing the attestation engagement
practitioner_vs_responsible_party.independence: The practitioner must be independent of the responsible party (required for examination and review; not required for AUP but must disclose if not independent)

three_types_of_attestation_engagements.description: SSAE allows three types of attestation engagements, each providing a different level of assurance.

hierarchy.examination: REASONABLE (high) assurance - similar to an audit
hierarchy.review: LIMITED (moderate) assurance - similar to a review under SSARS
hierarchy.agreed_upon_procedures_AUP: NO assurance - just report findings from specified procedures

procedures.examination: Sufficient procedures to reduce risk to appropriately low level - may include testing, inspection, confirmation, observation, inquiry, analytical, recalculation
procedures.AUP: ONLY the procedures agreed upon with the engaging party - can be any procedures

independence.AUP: NOT required (but must disclose if not independent)

report_conclusion.examination: 'In our opinion, [subject matter] is presented in accordance with [criteria]' OR '[assertion] is fairly stated in all material respects'
report_conclusion.review: 'Based on our review, we are not aware of any material modifications that should be made to [assertion/subject matter]'
report_conclusion.AUP: NO conclusion or opinion - just listing of procedures and findings

suitable_criteria_required.AUP: NOT necessarily - procedures are specified by engaging party

three_types_of_attestation_engagements.exam_strategy: Know this comparison table cold. Many exam questions ask about differences between examination, review, and AUP attestation engagements.

examination_engagements.description: An examination engagement provides REASONABLE ASSURANCE (high level of assurance) on whether the subject matter is in accordance with suitable criteria, or whether management's assertion is fairly stated.

assurance_level.comparison_to_audit: Similar to an audit - provides positive conclusion
assurance_level.conclusion_format: POSITIVE conclusion - 'In our opinion...' (similar to audit opinion)

procedures.description: The practitioner performs sufficient procedures to obtain reasonable assurance. The specific procedures depend on the subject matter but may include:
typical_procedures: Testing of controls (if subject matter is control effectiveness)
procedures.sufficiency: Procedures must be sufficient to reduce attestation risk to an appropriately low level (similar to audit risk in an audit)
procedures.nature_timing_extent: Practitioner determines nature, timing, and extent of procedures based on risk assessment

examination_engagements.independence_requirement: The practitioner MUST be independent to perform an examination engagement

required_elements: Title including the word 'Independent'
Identification of subject matter or assertion
Identification of responsible party
Statement that examination was conducted per SSAE
Statement about practitioner's responsibilities and responsible party's responsibilities
Description of nature of examination (but not detailed procedures)
Statement about inherent limitations
Practitioner's opinion/conclusion
Signature and date

opinion_wording_options.option_1_on_subject_matter: 'In our opinion, [subject matter] is presented in accordance with [criteria] in all material respects.'
opinion_wording_options.option_2_on_assertion: 'In our opinion, management's assertion that [assertion] is fairly stated in all material respects.'

modified_conclusions.qualified: When subject matter does not conform to criteria in a material respect but effect is not pervasive
modified_conclusions.adverse: When subject matter does not conform to criteria and the effect is material and pervasive
modified_conclusions.disclaimer: When unable to obtain sufficient evidence (scope limitation) and effects are material and pervasive

common_examination_topics: Internal control over financial reporting (SOX 404 attestation)
Effectiveness of controls at a service organization (SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2)
examination_engagements.exam_focus: Examination = reasonable assurance = positive opinion. Similar to audit but on subject matter other than historical FS.

review_engagements.description: A review engagement provides LIMITED ASSURANCE on whether any material modifications should be made to the subject matter or assertion to be in accordance with suitable criteria.

assurance_level.comparison_to_ssars_review: Similar to SSARS review of financial statements - provides negative assurance
assurance_level.conclusion_format: NEGATIVE conclusion - 'We are not aware of any material modifications...' (similar to SSARS review)

procedures.description: Review procedures are primarily INQUIRY and ANALYTICAL procedures. Less extensive than examination.
typical_procedures: Inquire about criteria and how subject matter conforms to criteria
Perform analytical procedures to identify unusual relationships
Obtain written representations from responsible party
procedures.what_is_not_performed: Reviews generally do NOT include testing, confirmation, observation, or inspection (unless something appears questionable)
procedures.comparison_to_examination: Review procedures are significantly less extensive than examination procedures

review_engagements.independence_requirement: The practitioner MUST be independent to perform a review engagement

required_elements: Title including 'Independent'
Identification of subject matter or assertion
Statement that review was conducted per SSAE
Statement that review is substantially less in scope than examination
Practitioner's conclusion
Signature and date
review_report.conclusion_wording: 'Based on our review, we are not aware of any material modifications that should be made to [subject matter/assertion] in order for it to be in accordance with [criteria].'
review_report.negative_assurance: The conclusion provides NEGATIVE assurance - states what the practitioner is NOT aware of, rather than providing positive opinion

when_review_is_appropriate: Engaging party needs some assurance but reasonable assurance is not necessary or cost-effective
Subject matter is not highly complex or risky
review_engagements.exam_note: Attestation review is similar to SSARS review - limited assurance, inquiry + analytical procedures, negative conclusion. But SSAE review is for subject matter OTHER than historical FS.

agreed_upon_procedures_engagements.description: An agreed-upon procedures (AUP) engagement involves the practitioner performing SPECIFIC PROCEDURES that have been AGREED UPON with the engaging party and reporting the FINDINGS. NO assurance is provided.

assurance_level.not_an_opinion: The practitioner does NOT provide an opinion, conclusion, or any assurance
assurance_level.just_findings: The report simply lists the procedures performed and the findings. USERS draw their own conclusions.

procedures.who_determines: The ENGAGING PARTY (client or intended users) specifies which procedures to perform
procedures.practitioner_role: The practitioner performs ONLY the agreed-upon procedures - nothing more, nothing less
procedures.can_be_any_procedures: The procedures can be anything agreed upon - testing, confirmation, observation, inspection, inquiry, computation, comparison, etc.
procedures.no_additional_procedures: Even if the practitioner notices something unusual, they do NOT perform additional procedures beyond what was agreed upon (unless they're asked to do so)

independence_not_required.rule: The practitioner does NOT need to be independent for AUP engagements
independence_not_required.disclosure: If NOT independent, must disclose in the AUP report
independence_not_required.rationale: Since no assurance is provided and users are specifying the procedures, independence is less critical. Users draw their own conclusions from findings.

required_elements: Title
Identification of specified parties (who can use the report)
Identification of subject matter
Statement that AUP engagement was conducted per SSAE
Statement of practitioner's responsibilities
Statement that engagement was conducted based on procedures agreed upon
LIST of procedures performed
LIST of findings for each procedure
Statement that NO opinion or conclusion is provided
Statement that report is restricted to specified parties
Signature and date

key_characteristics.lists_procedures_and_findings: Report includes detailed list of procedures and what was found for each procedure
key_characteristics.no_conclusion: Report does NOT include opinion, conclusion, or assurance statement
key_characteristics.restricted_use: Report is typically RESTRICTED to the parties who agreed upon the procedures (not for general distribution)
key_characteristics.findings_only: Practitioners reports only FINDINGS - does not interpret or provide conclusion

aup_report.example_excerpt: 'We compared the sales amounts listed in Column A to the sales amounts in the general ledger for January 2024. The amounts agreed for 48 of 50 items tested. For 2 items (Invoice #1523 and #1687), the amounts in Column A were $500 higher than the general ledger amounts.'
aup_report.what_report_does_not_say: Report does NOT say whether the differences are material, whether additional items might have differences, or what users should conclude. Just states findings.

when_aup_is_appropriate: Users have specific questions and want specific procedures performed
Users are sophisticated and can interpret findings themselves
Subject matter is narrow or specific
Users want to control which procedures are performed (not relying on practitioner's judgment)
Cost-effective alternative when full assurance not needed
Regulatory or contractual requirements specify certain procedures

restricted_use.description: AUP reports are generally RESTRICTED USE - only for the parties who agreed upon the procedures
restricted_use.reason: Other parties who didn't participate in agreeing on procedures might misunderstand or misuse the findings
restricted_use.report_language: Report includes restriction: 'This report is intended solely for the information and use of [specified parties] and is not intended to be and should not be used by anyone other than these specified parties.'

exam_emphasis: AUP provides NO assurance - just findings
Independence NOT required (but must disclose if not independent)
Report lists procedures and findings - no conclusion

comparison_to_ssars.description: It's critical to understand when to apply SSAE vs. SSARS.

ssars_applies.what: SSARS applies to services on HISTORICAL FINANCIAL STATEMENTS of NON-PUBLIC companies
ssars_applies.services: Preparation, compilation, review of historical financial statements
ssars_applies.example: CPA reviews the 2024 financial statements of ABC Company (non-public) - use SSARS

ssae_applies.what: SSAE applies to attestation on SUBJECT MATTER OTHER THAN historical FS, or special reports
ssae_applies.services: Examination, review, agreed-upon procedures on various subject matter
examples: CPA examines ABC Company's internal controls - use SSAE
CPA performs AUP on ABC Company's sales data - use SSAE
CPA reviews ABC Company's compliance with debt covenants - use SSAE

comparison_to_ssars.exam_trap: Don't confuse SSARS review with SSAE review. SSARS = historical FS. SSAE = other subject matter. Both provide limited assurance with negative conclusion, but different standards.

soc_reports.description: SOC (Service Organization Controls) reports are a common type of SSAE attestation. They address controls at service organizations that provide services to user entities.

why_soc_reports_exist.service_organizations: Many companies outsource functions to service organizations (e.g., payroll processing, IT hosting, cloud services, benefits administration)
why_soc_reports_exist.user_entity_auditor_concern: When a user entity outsources a function, the user entity's auditor needs to understand controls at the service organization (because they affect the user entity's financial reporting)
why_soc_reports_exist.solution: Service organization obtains SOC report from its auditor, which user entity's auditor can rely upon

soc_1.full_name: SOC 1 - Report on Controls at a Service Organization Relevant to User Entities' Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
soc_1.purpose: Addresses controls relevant to USER ENTITIES' FINANCIAL REPORTING
soc_1.who_uses: User entity auditors (CPAs auditing the user entity's financial statements)
soc_1.criteria: Usually management's description of the service organization's system and controls
soc_1.example: Payroll processing company gets SOC 1 report. User entity's auditor reviews the SOC 1 report to understand payroll controls.

type_1.description: Report on controls AT A POINT IN TIME
type_1.procedures: Service auditor tests DESIGN of controls as of a specific date
type_1.opinion: Opinion on whether controls are suitably designed as of the specified date
type_1.limitation: Does NOT provide evidence about operating effectiveness over a period of time

type_2.description: Report on controls OVER A PERIOD OF TIME
type_2.procedures: Service auditor tests DESIGN and OPERATING EFFECTIVENESS of controls over a period (usually 6-12 months)
type_2.opinion: Opinion on whether controls are suitably designed AND operating effectively over the period
type_2.more_useful: Type 2 is more useful to user auditors because it provides evidence over time, not just at a point in time

soc_1.exam_importance: SOC 1 is the most important for financial statement auditors. Know the difference between Type 1 (point in time, design only) and Type 2 (period of time, design and operating effectiveness).

soc_2.full_name: SOC 2 - Report on Controls at a Service Organization Relevant to Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, or Privacy (Trust Services Criteria)
soc_2.purpose: Addresses controls relevant to TRUST SERVICES CRITERIA (security, availability, etc.) - NOT specifically financial reporting
soc_2.who_uses: Management of user entities, regulators, business partners, customers - not primarily for auditors
trust_services_criteria: Security - system is protected against unauthorized access
Availability - system is available for operation and use as committed
Processing Integrity - system processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, authorized
Privacy - personal information is collected, used, retained, disclosed, and disposed properly
soc_2.type_1_and_type_2: Like SOC 1, SOC 2 reports can be Type 1 (point in time) or Type 2 (period of time). Type 2 is more common and useful.
soc_2.restricted_use: SOC 2 reports are RESTRICTED USE - only for specified parties (not for general distribution)
soc_2.example: Cloud hosting company gets SOC 2 report to demonstrate to customers that security and availability controls are effective.

soc_3.full_name: SOC 3 - Trust Services Report for Service Organizations
soc_3.purpose: General use report on Trust Services Criteria - can be distributed publicly
soc_3.criteria: AICPA Trust Services Criteria (same as SOC 2)
soc_3.key_difference_from_soc_2: SOC 3 is GENERAL USE (not restricted). Does NOT include detailed description of tests or results - just the service auditor's opinion.
soc_3.less_detail: Much less detailed than SOC 2 - basically just says 'controls met the criteria' without describing specific controls or tests
soc_3.example: Service organization publishes SOC 3 report on its website for marketing purposes

exam_comparison.soc_1: For FINANCIAL REPORTING controls - used by auditors
exam_comparison.soc_2: For TRUST SERVICES controls - RESTRICTED use
exam_comparison.soc_3: For TRUST SERVICES controls - GENERAL use (less detail than SOC 2)
exam_comparison.type_1_vs_type_2: Type 1 = point in time (design only). Type 2 = period of time (design + operating effectiveness)

exam_tips: Know that SOC 1 is for financial reporting controls, SOC 2/3 are for trust services criteria
Type 2 is more useful than Type 1 because it covers operating effectiveness over time
SOC 2 is restricted use, SOC 3 is general use
All SOC reports are EXAMINATIONS (reasonable assurance) under SSAE

prospective_financial_information.description: SSAE also covers engagements involving prospective financial information (forecasts and projections).

forecast_vs_projection.forecast: Prospective financial information based on EXPECTED conditions and EXPECTED courses of action (management's best estimate of what WILL happen)
forecast_vs_projection.projection: Prospective financial information based on one or more HYPOTHETICAL assumptions (what COULD happen IF certain assumptions occur)
forecast_vs_projection.example_forecast: ABC Company forecasts revenue of $10M for 2025 based on expected market conditions
forecast_vs_projection.example_projection: ABC Company projects revenue of $10M IF they acquire competitor XYZ (hypothetical assumption)

distribution.forecast_general_use: Forecasts can be for GENERAL use (any user)
distribution.projection_limited_use: Projections are generally for LIMITED use only (parties negotiating directly with responsible party)
distribution.reason: Projections are based on hypothetical assumptions and could be misunderstood by general users

practitioner_services.examination: Practitioner can examine forecasts or projections - provides opinion on whether assumptions are reasonable and presentation follows AICPA guidelines
practitioner_services.compilation: Practitioner can compile forecasts or projections - assembles prospective info but provides no assurance
practitioner_services.agreed_upon_procedures: Practitioner can perform AUP on forecasts/projections

prospective_financial_information.exam_note: Prospective financial information is lightly tested. Know the basic distinction: forecast = expected, projection = hypothetical.

pro_forma_financial_information.description: Pro forma financial information shows what historical FS would have looked like IF a transaction had occurred (e.g., acquisition, disposition).
pro_forma_financial_information.example: Company A acquires Company B. Pro forma FS show what the combined entity would have looked like for the prior year.
pro_forma_financial_information.practitioner_service: Practitioner can perform examination or review of pro forma financial information under SSAE
pro_forma_financial_information.exam_note: Rarely tested - just know the concept exists

practice_problems.question:
For each scenario below, identify:
(1) Whether the engagement follows GAAS, SSARS, or SSAE
(2) What type of engagement is appropriate (audit, review, compilation, examination, AUP, etc.)
(3) Level of assurance provided

Scenario A: CPA engaged to report on XYZ Company's (non-public) compliance with debt covenants. Bank wants reasonable assurance.

Scenario B: CPA engaged to review the 2024 financial statements of ABC Company, a non-public company.

Scenario C: CPA engaged to perform specific procedures agreed upon with management on sales data for January 2025.

Scenario D: DEF Company (public) needs financial statement audit for SEC filing.

scenario_A.standards: SSAE - compliance with debt covenants is NOT historical financial statements, so not GAAS or SSARS
scenario_A.report_conclusion: 'In our opinion, XYZ Company complied with the debt covenants in all material respects during the year ended...'
scenario_A.procedures: Sufficient procedures to obtain reasonable assurance - may include testing compliance, examining loan agreement, recalculating covenant ratios, confirming with lender

scenario_B.standards: SSARS - review of historical financial statements for non-public company
scenario_B.report_conclusion: 'Based on my review, I am not aware of any material modifications that should be made to the financial statements...'
scenario_B.procedures: Inquiry and analytical procedures, management representation letter
scenario_B.not_ssae: Even though this is a 'review,' it's under SSARS (not SSAE) because it's historical FS for non-public company

scenario_C.standards: SSAE - agreed-upon procedures on data (not financial statement audit or review)
scenario_C.report_format: Lists procedures performed and findings for each procedure. No opinion or conclusion.
scenario_C.procedures: ONLY the procedures agreed upon with management
scenario_C.independence_required: NO (but must disclose if not independent)
scenario_C.restricted_use: Report likely restricted to management (parties who agreed on procedures)

scenario_D.standards: GAAS (and PCAOB standards since public company)
scenario_D.report_opinion: 'In our opinion, the financial statements present fairly...'
scenario_D.procedures: Full audit procedures - confirmation, observation, testing, inspection, analytical, inquiry
scenario_D.not_ssae: Financial statement audit follows GAAS, not SSAE

solution.key_takeaway: GAAS = FS audits. SSARS = FS reviews/compilations for non-public. SSAE = everything else (other subject matter, AUP, examinations/reviews on non-FS topics).

practice_problems.question:
A cloud hosting service provider wants to demonstrate to its customers that security and availability controls are effective.

Required:
1. Which type of SOC report is most appropriate?
2. Should it be Type 1 or Type 2?
3. Can the report be publicly distributed on the company's website?
4. What are the criteria used for the examination?
5. What level of assurance is provided?

part_1_soc_type.reasoning: The engagement addresses SECURITY and AVAILABILITY, which are Trust Services Criteria. SOC 1 addresses FINANCIAL REPORTING controls, which is not what's needed here. SOC 2 or SOC 3 both address Trust Services Criteria.

choice_between_2_and_3.soc_2: More detailed, restricted use report. Includes description of controls, tests performed, and results. Customers specified as users can access.
choice_between_2_and_3.soc_3: General use report. Can be publicly distributed. Less detailed - just states controls met criteria without describing specific tests.
choice_between_2_and_3.recommendation: If company wants to PUBLICLY distribute on website for marketing = SOC 3. If company wants to provide to SPECIFIC customers with detailed information = SOC 2.

reasoning.type_1: Report on controls at a POINT IN TIME - tests design only as of a specific date. Provides limited value because only addresses one moment in time.
reasoning.type_2: Report on controls OVER A PERIOD (usually 6-12 months) - tests design AND operating effectiveness. Much more useful to customers because demonstrates controls worked throughout the period.
reasoning.recommendation: Customers want assurance that controls are effective OVER TIME, not just on one day. Type 2 is almost always preferred for SOC 2 and SOC 3.

part_3_public_distribution.if_soc_2: NO - SOC 2 reports are RESTRICTED USE only. Can only be provided to specified parties who have understanding of service organization and criteria. Cannot be publicly distributed.
part_3_public_distribution.if_soc_3: YES - SOC 3 reports are GENERAL USE and can be publicly distributed, including on website.
part_3_public_distribution.choice: If company wants public distribution, must use SOC 3 (not SOC 2)

part_4_criteria.specific_criteria: Security and Availability (two of the five Trust Services Criteria)
part_4_criteria.all_five_criteria: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy
part_4_criteria.note: Company selects which of the five criteria are relevant. In this case, Security and Availability.

part_5_assurance.reasoning: All SOC reports (SOC 1, SOC 2, SOC 3) are EXAMINATION engagements under SSAE, which provide reasonable assurance (positive opinion)
part_5_assurance.opinion_format: 'In our opinion, the controls were suitably designed and operating effectively to meet the criteria...' (for Type 2)

solution.final_recommendation: For public distribution: SOC 3 Type 2 on Security and Availability using Trust Services Criteria, providing reasonable assurance. For restricted use with more detail: SOC 2 Type 2.

tip_1_ssae_vs_ssars_vs_gaas.description: Know when each set of standards applies
tip_1_ssae_vs_ssars_vs_gaas.gaas: Audits of historical financial statements (all companies)
tip_1_ssae_vs_ssars_vs_gaas.ssars: Preparation, compilation, review of historical FS for non-public companies
tip_1_ssae_vs_ssars_vs_gaas.ssae: Attestation on subject matter OTHER than historical FS - examinations, reviews, AUP on various subject matter
tip_1_ssae_vs_ssars_vs_gaas.exam_question: If question involves historical FS for non-public company = SSARS. If involves other subject matter = SSAE. If involves FS audit = GAAS.

tip_2_three_attestation_types.description: Memorize the three types and their characteristics
tip_2_three_attestation_types.examination: Reasonable assurance, positive opinion, extensive procedures, independence required
tip_2_three_attestation_types.review: Limited assurance, negative conclusion, inquiry + analytical, independence required
tip_2_three_attestation_types.aup: No assurance, findings only, agreed procedures, independence NOT required
tip_2_three_attestation_types.exam_strategy: If question asks about assurance level or procedures, apply this hierarchy

tip_3_soc_reports.description: Know the three types of SOC reports and when each is used
tip_3_soc_reports.soc_3: Trust Services Criteria - general use (can be public)
tip_3_soc_reports.type_1_vs_2: Type 1 = point in time. Type 2 = period of time (more useful)
tip_3_soc_reports.exam_question: If question asks about controls for auditor reliance = SOC 1. If about security/availability for customers = SOC 2 or 3.

tip_4_suitable_criteria.description: Remember that suitable criteria are required for examination and review (not for AUP)
tip_4_suitable_criteria.characteristics: Relevant, objective, measurable, complete, available to users
tip_4_suitable_criteria.exam_scenario: Question may ask if engagement can be accepted when criteria are missing or inappropriate - answer NO for examination/review, but AUP might still work

tip_5_independence.description: Independence required for examination and review, NOT for AUP
tip_5_independence.aup: Independence NOT required (but disclose if not independent)
tip_5_independence.exam_question: CPA not independent - which engagement can be performed? Answer: AUP (with disclosure), or compilation under SSARS

tip_6_aup_characteristics.no_assurance: NO opinion, conclusion, or assurance provided
tip_6_aup_characteristics.restricted_use: Report restricted to parties who agreed on procedures
tip_6_aup_characteristics.findings_only: Report lists procedures and findings - practitioner doesn't interpret
tip_6_aup_characteristics.exam_trap: AUP report does NOT include opinion or conclusion - if answer choice says 'practitioner expresses limited assurance' that's wrong for AUP

tip_7_negative_vs_positive_assurance.description: Know the difference in report wording
tip_7_negative_vs_positive_assurance.positive_assurance_examination: 'In our opinion, [subject matter] is...' - states what IS
tip_7_negative_vs_positive_assurance.negative_assurance_review: 'We are not aware of any material modifications...' - states what is NOT aware of
tip_7_negative_vs_positive_assurance.exam_question: Question may show report excerpt and ask engagement type - look for positive vs. negative language

common_exam_question_patterns.pattern: Which standards apply to this engagement? (GAAS, SSARS, SSAE)
common_exam_question_patterns.approach: FS audit = GAAS. FS review/compilation (non-public) = SSARS. Other subject matter = SSAE
Know assurance levels, procedures, independence requirements, report formats
SOC 1 = financial reporting. SOC 2 = trust services, restricted. SOC 3 = trust services, general use
Type 1 = point in time (design). Type 2 = period (design + operating effectiveness)

common_exam_question_patterns.pattern: Can practitioner accept engagement when [some issue]?
common_exam_question_patterns.approach: Check if suitable criteria exist (needed for exam/review). Check if independence required.

memorization_aids.independence: E-R require independence, AUP does not (ER Independent, AUP not)
memorization_aids.type_1_vs_2: Type 2 = Period (both start with 'p'). Type 1 = Point
memorization_aids.criteria_characteristics: ROMCA: Relevant, Objective, Measurable, Complete, Available

key_concepts: SSAE applies to attestation on subject matter OTHER than historical financial statements
Three types of attestation: Examination (reasonable assurance), Review (limited assurance), AUP (no assurance)
All attestation requires subject matter, assertions, and suitable criteria (except AUP may not need criteria)
Examination provides positive opinion, similar to audit but on different subject matter
Review provides negative conclusion, primarily inquiry and analytical procedures
AUP provides NO assurance - just lists procedures and findings. Independence not required.
SOC 1 = financial reporting controls for auditors. SOC 2 = trust services, restricted. SOC 3 = trust services, general use.
Type 1 SOC = point in time (design only). Type 2 SOC = period (design + operating effectiveness)
Independence required for examination and review, NOT for AUP (but must disclose)
critical_for_exam: Distinguish SSAE from SSARS and GAAS - SSAE is for subject matter other than historical FS
Know three attestation types: examination (high assurance), review (limited), AUP (none)
SOC 1 for financial reporting, SOC 2/3 for trust services
Type 2 more useful than Type 1 (period vs. point in time)
AUP = no assurance, restricted use, findings only, independence not required
Examination and review require suitable criteria; AUP does not necessarily
common_mistakes: Confusing SSAE review with SSARS review - SSAE is for non-FS subject matter
Thinking AUP provides limited assurance - it provides NO assurance
Thinking independence required for AUP - it's not (but must disclose if not independent)
Confusing SOC 1 (financial reporting) with SOC 2 (trust services)
Thinking SOC 2 can be publicly distributed - it cannot (restricted use). SOC 3 is for general use.
Forgetting that Type 2 reports cover operating effectiveness, Type 1 only design
